question.:question/problem:
$$
f(t,y)=⟨10 \cos{\left(t \right)},\,y,\,\text{_____}⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(t,y)$ above parametrizes the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as $\frac{x^{2}}{100}+\frac{z^{2}}{9}=1.$ What is the third component of $f?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the ellipse $\frac{x^{2}}{100}+\frac{z^{2}}{9}=1$ in the $xz$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,z⟩=⟨10 \cos{\left(t \right)},\,3 \sin{\left(t \right)}⟩,\quad t\in[0,2\pi),
$$

since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x^2}{100}+\frac{z^2}{9}&=\frac{(10 \cos{\left(t \right)})^2}{100}+\frac{(3 \sin{\left(t \right)})^2}{9}\\&=\cos^2 t+\sin^2 t\\&=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
f(t,y)=⟨x,y,z⟩=⟨10 \cos{\left(t \right)},\,y,\,3 \sin{\left(t \right)}⟩
$$

where $t\in[0,2\pi)$ and $y\in(-\infty,\infty)$.

Therefore, the third component of $f$ is $3 \sin{\left(t \right)}$.

question.:question/problem:
![](images/fe/fe940cfc33f258f90248d50ad9eefc4527589cdbe5836fd12ee53958f1b257f8.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the ellipse shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since our ellipse is centered at the origin and has semiaxes $1$ and $4,$ its equation is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}=1\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}=1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}\right) & =0 \\ 2x+\frac{2y}{16}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{y}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{16x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Since our ellipse is centered at $(-3,1)$ and has semiaxes $3$ and $4,$ its equation is given by

$$
\frac{(x-(-3))^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{{4}^{2}}=1\,⟹\,\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{16}=1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{16}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{9}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{16}\right) & =0 \\ \frac{2(x+3)}{9}+\frac{2(y-1)}{16}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{y-1}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2(x+3)}{9} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{16(x+3)}{9(y-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x + 4 y^{2}$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=-5\,i+2\,j.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(-5)^{2}+(2)^{2}}=\sqrt{29} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{29}}(-5\,i+2\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x + 4 y^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x + 4 y^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,8 y⟩ \\ ∇f(1,1) & =⟨1,8 (1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨1,8⟩\cdot ⟨- \frac{5 \sqrt{29}}{29},\frac{2 \sqrt{29}}{29}⟩ \\  & =\frac{(1)\cdot (-5)+(8)\cdot (2)}{\sqrt{29}} \\  & =\frac{11 \sqrt{29}}{29}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=4 x y$ at the point $(2,3)$ in the direction of the vector $v=-2\,i+1\,j.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(1)^{2}}=\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(-2\,i+1\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(4 x y),\frac{∂}{∂y}(4 x y)⟩ \\  & =⟨4 y,4 x⟩ \\ ∇f(2,3) & =⟨12,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(2,3) & =∇f(2,3)\cdot u \\  & =⟨12,8⟩\cdot ⟨- \frac{2 \sqrt{5}}{5},\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}⟩ \\  & =\frac{(12)\cdot (-2)+(8)\cdot (1)}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =- \frac{16 \sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x y$ at the point $(3,3)$ in the direction of the vector $v=\sqrt{3}\,i-1\,j.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=2 \\ u & =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}\,i-1\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(3,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x y),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x y)⟩ \\  & =⟨y,x⟩ \\ ∇f(3,3) & =⟨3,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(3,3) & =∇f(3,3)\cdot u \\  & =⟨3,3⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},- \frac{1}{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{(3)\cdot (\sqrt{3})+(3)\cdot (-1)}{2} \\  & =- \frac{3}{2} + \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=2 \left(x + 4 y^{2}\right)^{2}$ at the point $A(-3,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(0,3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨0,3⟩-⟨-3,1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,2⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(2)^{2}}}⟨3,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}⟨3,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2 \left(x + 4 y^{2}\right)^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(2 \left(x + 4 y^{2}\right)^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨4(x+4y^{2})\cdot 1,4(x+4y^{2})\cdot 8y⟩ \\  & =⟨4 x + 16 y^{2},32 y \left(x + 4 y^{2}\right)⟩ \\ ∇f(-3,1) & =⟨4 (-3) + 16 (1)^{2},32 (1) \left((-3) + 4 (1)^{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,32⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-3,1) & =∇f(-3,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨4,32⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{3 \sqrt{13}}{13},\frac{2 \sqrt{13}}{13}⟩ \\  & =\frac{(4)\cdot (3)+(32)\cdot (2)}{\sqrt{13}} \\  & =\frac{76 \sqrt{13}}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨-4,-4⟩-⟨0,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-4,-3⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(-3)^{2}}}⟨-4,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨-4,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(0,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(4 \left(x + y^{2}\right)^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(4 \left(x + y^{2}\right)^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨8(x+1y^{2})\cdot 1,8(x+1y^{2})\cdot 2y⟩ \\  & =⟨8 x + 8 y^{2},16 y \left(x + y^{2}\right)⟩ \\ ∇f(0,-1) & =⟨8 (0) + 8 (-1)^{2},16 (-1) \left((0) + (-1)^{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨8,-16⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(0,-1) & =∇f(0,-1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨8,-16⟩\cdot ⟨- \frac{4}{5},- \frac{3}{5}⟩ \\  & =\frac{(8)\cdot (-4)+(-16)\cdot (-3)}{5} \\  & =\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=3 \left(x + 3 y^{2}\right)^{2}$ at the point $A(-2,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-4,4).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨-4,4⟩-⟨-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,3⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(3)^{2}}}⟨-2,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}⟨-2,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(3 \left(x + 3 y^{2}\right)^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(3 \left(x + 3 y^{2}\right)^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨6(x+3y^{2})\cdot 1,6(x+3y^{2})\cdot 6y⟩ \\  & =⟨6 x + 18 y^{2},36 y \left(x + 3 y^{2}\right)⟩ \\ ∇f(-2,1) & =⟨6 (-2) + 18 (1)^{2},36 (1) \left((-2) + 3 (1)^{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨6,36⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-2,1) & =∇f(-2,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨6,36⟩\cdot ⟨- \frac{2 \sqrt{13}}{13},\frac{3 \sqrt{13}}{13}⟩ \\  & =\frac{(6)\cdot (-2)+(36)\cdot (3)}{\sqrt{13}} \\  & =\frac{96 \sqrt{13}}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$
